plan.title: Every reply was "Got it": thinking used the whole token budget

transcript.text: hey ZOH, so my back has apparently decided sitting 9 hours a day is a bad lifestyle choice lol. want to stretch every morning for like 10 min. never been good at sticking to stuff tho 😅

Hey, I'm ZOH! I'll help you get better at one thing with a small step a day, and 10 minutes of morning stretching for that back? Let's go. You can text "stop" anytime, and you can change how I coach just by telling me ("chill out", "push me harder"). What's your name?
lol "got it" is that all I get? 😂
Ha, you get way more than that from me. I'm in your corner on this back situation. Where will you stretch in the morning, and do you already have a spot, like a bedroom floor or a mat?

checks.reason: No markdown, hashtags or filler; reads as plain texting.
Upbeat and warm with one emoji-free, sincere tone; "Let's go" fits the pushy default.
Takes the stretching goal the tester raised and asks a name question as the intro requires.
Uses only what the tester said: back pain, 10 minutes, mornings.
Two sentences, within the one-to-three limit.
Plain text with no markdown or filler.
Warm and sincere ("I'm in your corner") without affection or a pile of emoji.
Asks where they'll stretch, a practical question that moves the plan forward.
Does not re-ask anything the tester already gave.
Makes no invented claims; references only the back issue the tester mentioned.
No wake or sleep question and no pushiness question.

conversation.reason: Neither ZOH text is "Got it", and there is no apology; both are real replies that move the stretching plan forward.

grade.summary: ZOH avoided the old "Got it" loop: its opener introduces itself, explains the small-step coaching, covers stop and style changes, and treats morning stretching as a valid start. Its reply to the tester's jab is a real, warm answer with no apology, and it asks one useful question about where they'll stretch.
